LEARNING PATH LESSON · COLORS & SHAPES · AGES 2 YEARS

Square — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson counts the square into your toddler’s world: four corners, one finger, and the boxy things in every room that were squares all along.

What is this?

A square is a shape with four equal sides and four corners — it sits still and does not roll, which is how your toddler’s hands will know it.

What does it mean?

Counting corners is the first counting-with-a-purpose most toddlers do: one, two, three, four, and the number belongs to the shape. Two words, one game.

What does the child need to know?

The square’s party trick is stillness — it does not roll, unlike its friend the circle. Demonstrate both once and the difference moves into the fingers.

Why this matters

Squares are the most-seen shape in any house: windows, cushions, books, crackers. Catching them in the wild turns furniture into flashcards.

What it teaches

Counting to four with a target, corner-spotting as visual analysis, and the roll-versus-still property contrast that organises the shape world.

Words to learn

squarefourcornerssidesstillwindow

Say this to your child

“"Square! One, two, three, four — four corners! Can you count them with me? Push it… it sits still. Squares do not roll. Can you find a square in this room? Count its corners!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and say square, then count the corners together with one finger — one, two, three, four.
  2. Trace the sides slowly and count them too: four sides, four corners, the same number twice.
  3. Prove the stillness: roll the ball (it goes) and push the square block (it stays). Squares sit still.
  4. Hunt squares in the room — a window, a cushion, a book cover — counting corners on each find.
  5. Hand out square crackers at snack time and count the corners again, with eating allowed as the final step.

Look closer at the picture

This card is the square card — one boxy shape filling the picture, with the word square printed for toddlers. Ask your child to count its corners with one finger.

Ask your child

"What shape is this card?" "How many corners does it have?" "Does the square roll?" "Can you find a square window?"

What your child can say or do

A solemn corner-count that reaches two, three or the full four — every version counts. Some toddlers will push the block across the rug, watch it stop, and announce still! — property language blooming.

Out in the real world

Windows, floor tiles, biscuits, waffle grids and picture frames keep squares in view all day. The cracker version is the only one that disappears at the end.

Try it together

Corner count parade: walk the room touching four-cornered things — table, cushion, book — and count to four at each one. Counting rides on the walking, and the room does the supplying.

Understanding check

Ask what shape the card is and how many corners it has. A square plus any honest corner-count passes. The push test settles the rest: a still square, named as still, is the full diploma.

Parent tips

Count with one slow finger, not a fast hand — slow tracing is what teaches the shape. Keep the roll comparison to one line; the square’s stillness needs the circle as its foil.

Staying safe

Corner-counting tours pass real furniture with real corners at toddler-eye height — the counting finger is welcome, the running is not, and the coffee table keeps score.

This lesson pairs with the Square flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Colors & Shapes (Toddler 3).
